newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh denies giving land transit to India.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh denies giving land transit to India.

text.p: Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad on Thursday denied reports that his government had offered a land transit to neighbouring India.
"We have not committed anything to India as yet. It's their proposal to have land routes through Bangladesh to transport goods among various Indian states," he told a news conference.
"We have only decided to take appropriate measures and the matter (transit) will be settled in parliament."
Bangladesh is surrounded on three sides by India and they share more than 1,700 miles (2,720 km) of border.

The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) has called for a general strike on Sunday to protest what it called the government's decision to offer transit to India and other deals that might "jeopardise the country's sovereignty."
The BNP, led by ex-prime minister Begun Khaleda Zia, also accused the government of letting India use Bangladeshi land to suppress a so-called "freedom struggle" in India's Assam and Tripura states.
Azad said Bangladesh would never support any separatist movement. "Neither shall we allow anyone to use our land for terrorist activities in other countries."
"But to strengthen the country's economy, we will have to do anything feasible. It's a must for us to move forward," he said.

"I don't see any harm in developing and improving communication systems among the SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) member countries," Azad added. "There could be transit facilities for growth of trade."
SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
Hasina, who took office in June, has already signed a 30-year treaty with India for sharing of the Ganges river.
Azad said India had also agreed to allow Nepal a land transit for transporting goods to Bangladesh.

He said the opposition was trying to mislead people by saying the transit link would undermine Bangladesh's sovereignty. "It's the wrong line it has taken, and that will go against the interest of the nation and the region," he said.
